title: The Canticle of the Sun
hook: Francis, nearly blind, praises God for brother sun, sister water, even sister death

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernard's four loves: self for self, God for self, God for God, self for God. Your line was love for love's sake. Did you do something with no return? Day two hundred sixty-nine.

Picture a small hut beside a chapel in Italy, in the year 1225. Inside, a man in his early forties is lying in the dark. His eyes are so diseased that daylight is agony, so they've shaded him from it. He's in constant pain. He sleeps badly; tradition says the mice ran over him at night. He has given away everything he ever owned. And in that hut, half blind, sick, and poor, he writes a song thanking God for the sun. His name is Francis of Assisi. Today: the Canticle of the Sun.
screen: `A HUT IN ITALY, 1225.` → `DAYLIGHT IS AGONY.` → `A SONG FOR THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Francis was the son of a rich cloth merchant who gave it all up to live in poverty, preach, and care for lepers. By 1225 he was worn out and nearly blind, and near the end of his life he composed this song. He didn't write it in Latin, the church's language. He wrote it in the everyday language of his region, and it's often counted among the earliest poems in Italian. It begins with praise to the Most High, and then it goes through creation like a family roll call. Praised be you, my Lord, with all your creatures, especially Sir Brother Sun, who brings the day. For Sister Moon and the stars. For Brother Wind and the air. For Sister Water, who is, he says, very useful and humble and precious and pure. For Brother Fire, bright and strong. For our Sister Mother Earth, who feeds us. Notice: brother and sister. Not resources. Not scenery. Family. Francis isn't worshipping the sun. He's praising God for it, and treating it as kin. Later he added a verse praising those who forgive for love, and the story goes that he sent friars to sing it to settle a quarrel between the bishop and the mayor of Assisi. And at the very end, knowing he was dying, he added one more: praised be you, my Lord, for our Sister Bodily Death, from whom no one living can escape. Sister death. Not an enemy. Part of the family too. He died in 1226. In 2015, Pope Francis took the song's opening words, Laudato si', praised be you, as the title of his letter on caring for the earth.
screen: `IN THE PEOPLE'S LANGUAGE.` · `BROTHER SUN, SISTER WATER.` · `KIN, NOT SCENERY.` · `EVEN SISTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise one element. Choose one: the sun, water, or fire. If you can, go to it. Stand in a patch of light, or run water over your hands, or look at a candle or a stove flame. Feel it on your skin. Think of it for a moment as a brother or sister, not a thing. If you pray, you can use Francis's words: praised be you, my Lord, for sister water. The bell holds the time.
The Canticle of the Sun. Francis's song praising God for brother sun, sister water, and at the last, sister death.
screen: `THE CANTICLE OF THE SUN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: praised be, for sister water. Today, every time you turn on a tap, let it be a tiny thank-you. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Christians sing versions of Francis's Canticle, including the hymn 'All Creatures of Our God and King', and Franciscans pray it as part of their tradition of caring for creation.

myth: Francis wrote the Canticle in Latin
he wrote it in the everyday language of his region, an early poem in Italian.
he praised God for the sun, and treated it as a brother.
he wrote it while nearly blind and ill
near the end of his life, in 1225, shaded from the daylight.

fork.setup: you're Francis. you're dying. the song is almost finished. what do you add?
options: a verse praising God for sister death.
fork.reveal: he added praise for Sister Bodily Death, from whom no one living can escape. not an enemy; family.

original.note: old Umbrian Italian, close to Latin: praised be you, my Lord.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty nature poem by a gentle saint.
what it means: a dying, nearly blind man calling sun, water and even death his family, and praising God for each.
what a scholar hears: one of the earliest poems in Italian; and the little word per, which can mean praised for, by, or through your creatures, and scholars still argue which.

sources.ref: Francis of Assisi, Canticle of the Creatures (Cantico di Frate Sole), c. 1225

notes: The Canticle is paraphrased in English (no public-domain translation on the validator's list); the opening Umbrian words are in the original game.
'The mice ran over him at night' is from the Assisi Compilation / Mirror of Perfection; the script says 'tradition says'.
The pardon verse and the bishop–mayor quarrel, and the death verse added near his death, are from early Franciscan sources; confirm.
The translation of Sister Water's four qualities (utile, humile, pretiosa, casta) as 'useful, humble, precious and pure' — casta is often 'chaste'; confirm.
The 'per' debate (for / by / through) is in the trapdoor; confirm framing.
